messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Kofi

Kofi was thirty-two when the war came to his neighborhood in Freetown. He had been a teacher then, unmarried, living with his mother in a modest house three streets back from the main road. On the morning of January 6th, 1999, he woke to the sound of automatic weapons and the smell of smoke. The rebels had breached the city's eastern perimeter during the night. By afternoon, soldiers were moving through the residential quarters, and Kofi, along with a dozen neighbors sheltering in a nearby compound, made the choice to run toward the university grounds, where they believed peacekeepers were stationed. They never made it. Two blocks from safety, a building ahead of them caught fire—a petrol station, or perhaps a house where fuel had been stored—and the flames spread with terrifying speed across the street, cutting off their route. Kofi and four others doubled back into the maze of side streets, separated from the rest. In the chaos, a young boy, no more than ten, who had been running alongside them, was shot. Kofi carried him for two blocks before the child died in his arms. He made it to the university alone. Forty-three people from his neighborhood did not.

For fifteen years after the war ended, Kofi built a life of deliberate normalcy. He emigrated to the United States at thirty-five, retrained as a park ranger, and took a position managing a large state forest in the Pacific Northwest. The work suited him—solitude, structure, the illusion of control. But in the past three years, the symptoms had become impossible to ignore. Any criticism from his supervisor, even the gentlest correction about a maintenance report or a protocol deviation, sent him into a spiral of shame and anger. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally corrupt, that his survival while others perished was a mark of cowardice or complicity he could never wash away. When his supervisor had suggested last spring that Kofi needed to spend more time in the field doing prescribed burns—a routine part of forest management—Kofi had felt the criticism as an accusation, and within weeks, he had begun to isolate. He stopped answering calls from the two colleagues who had tried to befriend him. He avoided the ranger station entirely, claiming illness, until his supervisor grew concerned enough to mandate a fitness-for-duty evaluation.

The prescribed burns were the real turning point. Fire had become a trigger—not just the memory of that January morning, but the very sight of flames in any form. When Kofi was required to oversee a controlled burn in a section of old-growth forest, the smell of smoke and the crackling advance of the fire line sent him into a state of hypervigilance that lasted for days. He couldn't sleep that night or the next. His mind raced with catastrophic interpretations: the fire would escape containment, people would die because of his incompetence, he would be responsible for another tragedy. He was certain that any delay in the burn crew's response to a flare-up meant disaster was unfolding, that something terrible was about to happen. The inability to relax, even sitting in his apartment afterward with all doors locked and the windows closed, was suffocating. He found himself reaching for alcohol more frequently—a beer or two in the evening became a nightly ritual, then two became four. He also began to avoid anything that resembled authority or enforcement: he stopped watching news broadcasts, avoided police checkpoints, and refused to attend a community safety meeting at his apartment complex because he couldn't bear the sight of the uniformed officers stationed outside.

The isolation deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally damaged and unfit for human connection. In the quiet of his apartment, alone with his thoughts, the guilt consumed him—why had that boy died and not him? What had he done, or failed to do, that made him worthy of survival? The more he drank, the more he withdrew, the more his sense of isolation crystallized into a felt certainty that he was marked, separated from normal life by something irreversible. Being in nature, which had once been his refuge, had become another minefield. A hike through the forest—something he used to do for solace—now triggered the same hypervigilance, the same sense that he was back in those streets, that danger was imminent. Even the sight of a distant brush fire on the news would send him into a state of dread that lingered for hours. The drinking helped briefly, dulling the edge, but it also meant he was no longer sleeping, and the exhaustion fed back into his threat sensitivity—every unexpected sound at night felt like a warning, every delay in a phone call from his mother felt like proof that something catastrophic was happening.

Three weeks ago, his supervisor informed him that if he did not complete a mental health evaluation and begin treatment, his position would be terminated. Kofi finally called a therapist. He sits now in the waiting room, hands trembling slightly, uncertain whether he can trust anyone with the truth of what he carries—the guilt, the shame, the conviction that he is fundamentally broken and that the world is far more dangerous than anyone else seems to understand.

violation_explanations: Negative appraisals (his belief that he is fundamentally corrupt, damaged, and unfit) are present throughout the vignette, and triggers (fire, smoke, authority figures, news broadcasts) are clearly identified, but no paragraph conveys that his negative appraisals lead to or activate his triggers; the causal direction runs the opposite way (triggers activate appraisals) or operates independently.
